Subject: downsizing algorithm
--text follows this line--

-------------------------------------------------------
BASE COMPUTE_TIMING ALGORITHM

Recall the "compute_timing" algorithm (simplified):

* initialize all stored delays to zero

* start with all timing sources (external inputs, clocks, or
  tied nets), assigning delay = 0

* propagate delay on this net:

	* add net delay 

	* if the inport is a timing destination (non-clock edge 
	  of "flipflop" (...&tc, eg ram),
		* if delay > design-long-delay, 
		  set design-long->path = current path

		* continue with next inport on this net

	* propagate delay on inport->instance:

		* find all timing arcs begining at the inport; 
		  for each timing arc:	
			* compute the delay across the timing arc
			* set delay =  inport delay + timing arc delay
			* if delay > outport long-delay, 
			    set outport long-delay = delay
			    set	outport's long-path-inport = inport
			* mark this arc as traversed
			* find all arcs *ending* at this outport;
			  if all have been traversed, propagate delay
			  to the net connected to the outport

-------------------------------------------------------
CHANGES TO THE BASE COMPUTE_TIMING ALGORITHM

Now add a new data item on each outport, "instance-long-delay", 
initially zero, and ammend the "compute_timing" algorithm:

* When we encounter a timing destination, walk back along the current
  path; for each instance, 
	* if path-delay > instance-long-delay,
	  set instance-long-delay = path-delay

So at the conclusion of compute-timing, each instance is marked with
the path-delay of the longest path it particpates in.  The design
long-path-delay is also known, as usual. The difference between the
two delays is the "instance-timing-slack". 

-------------------------------------------------------
BASIC DOWNSIZE-NONCRITICAL-INSTANCES ALGORITHM

Parameters:  minimum-instance-timing-slack, maximum-acceptable-slope

* mark all instances as "not-resized"

* until we make a pass without downsizeing any instances:		

	* compute_timing to find all instance-slack as above

	* Walk over all instances 
	  ... for the sake of arguement, breadth-first tree walk backwards
		from timing destinations  
	  For each instance:

		* if instance has been resized, continue

		* if instance-timing-slack <
		  minimimum-instance-timing-slack, continue

		* if no next-smaller-cell, continue

		* compute output slope with next-smaller-cell and
		  existing loads; 
		  if > maximum-acceptable-slope, continue;


		* replace instance with next-smaller-cell and compute 
		  additional-local-delay (change in delay from input
		  of driving instance to output of driven instance)

		* if instance-slack - additional-local-delay <
		  minimum-instance-timing-slack, 
		  restore previous cell and continue

		* walk back over tree of driver gates; for each,
		  set instance-slack = instance-slack -
			additional-local-delay  

* (optional) 
	* collect clones & save to sue
	* redo DPC

-------------------------------------------------------
DISCUSSION

Taking the used-up slack out of the entire backtree of each instance
guarantees that we won't increase the long path by spending the same
slack on two instance in a path; but obviously we will be charging it
to a large number of gates that don't deserve it.  However, when we
do compute-timing in the next pass, that reduced slack will be charged
correctly.  The justification for this is that in a large design with 
many paths, we will be able to make a large number of adjustments
purely by local inspection before having to take the hit of a global
retiming. 

Note that we could also charge the additional-local-delay to all
instances in the foretree as well the backtree; if this is done, then
I claim the order of downsizeing instances is not critical in the
sense that the algorithm is stable and will not impact the
design-long-path.  It *does* make a difference to the result in the
sense that the set of instances that get downsized is dependent on the
ordering; gates early in the ordering are more likely to be
successfully donwsized.  Possible other orderings: 

	* by cell type, in order of desireability of downsizing;
	  .... ie, in order of decreasing difference in size or power
	  drain between this size and the next size smaller 

	* decreasing order of instance-timing-slack
	  this would tend to even out the slack, which conceivably
	  could make life easier for the router
		
-------------------------------------------------------
A MORE POWERFUL ALGORITHM

It would be possible to sharpen this method to accurately account for 
the used-up slack by storing the set of paths that pass through each
instance. (note, a stored path, as implemented in Speedy, includes the
timing delays along that path...) Then, for each path in the set,

	* recalulate the timing along that path, and note the new
	  path-delay 

	* for each instance on the path, 
	  if the path-delay > instance-long-delay,
	  set instance-long-delay = path-delay

With this method, it should not be necessary to iterate, since the
instance-slack is always accurate (what it would be if compute-timing
were done). 

Note that this algorithm is inherently independent of instance order.


-------------------------------------------------------
IMPLICATIONS FOR GLOBAL ROUTER

Note that the extended global routing algorithm has the same basic
problem.

At the conclusion of the present steiner-based global routing
algorithm, some gridboxes (global routing cells) are known to be
over-congested.  It is possible to reduce congestion by routing 
some segments around congested areas; this would necessarily involve 
adding length, and therefore delay.  In order to avoid impacting
timing, we would like to select segments that have maximum slack,
which can be computed using the same algorithm as above.
